stories.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The embrace of Russia by Niger, and other Sahel states, has been seen as a rejection of the post-colonial Western powers By Simi Jolaoso Africa correspondent Published 6 hours ago When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia. Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport. Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny". "This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule." The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.

stories.summary: African Development Bank and Axian Launch Digital Finance Programme to Support 34,000 Women-Led Businesses in Africa 2 September 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) AXIAN Group and the African Development Bank have launched a major women's financial inclusion programme to expand access to finance and business support for more than 34,000 women-led enterprises in five African countries. Supported by the African Development Bank's Affirmative Finance Action for Women in Africa (AFAWA) initiative and the Women Entrepreneurs Finance Initiative (We-Fi), the programme aims to address one of the biggest constraints facing women-owned businesses in Africa - limited access to finance. Africa has the highest rate of female entrepreneurship worldwide, yet women entrepreneurs still face an estimated $49 billion financing gap. The programme will be implemented through AXIAN Group's digital financial services platforms, Mixx and Mvola, which integrate digital lending, financial literacy training, business development services and digital inclusion initiatives to help women entrepreneurs grow their businesses and improve their access to formal financial services. It comprises two complementary components.

What began as a slide back into authoritarianism has hardened into systematic repression of civil society organizations, journalists, political opponents, independent lawyers, and migrants. Shrinking Civic Space and Crackdown on Civil Society Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines President Saied has repeatedly accused civil society organizations of serving foreign interests, calling them "traitors" and "mercenaries." Since May 2024, Tunisian authorities have systematically targeted civil society organizations through arbitrary arrests, detentions, financial and criminal investigations, and administrative suspensions. Speaking during the 59th Passing-Out Parade for Administration Police recruits at the National Police College in Embakasi, Nairobi, Ruto said the new uniforms should not be viewed as an isolated project. "The new uniforms for general duty officers that we unveiled last week must be understood within this broader reform program," Ruto said. "It is not a standalone intervention, but part of the comprehensive transformation of the National Police Service arising from the reform process." Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The President said the uniforms were developed after consultations with police officers and members of the public. According to Ruto, the new design was meant to improve the professional identity of officers while also considering their operational needs and dignity. "The uniform itself emerged from consultation with police officers and with the Kenyan public," he said. He acknowledged that a uniform by itself could not change the police service, but argued that it plays a role in building a more professional force. "A uniform alone cannot transform policing, but professional identity and pride are part of building a modern, disciplined, and effective police service," Ruto said. The President also appeared to welcome scrutiny of the wider police reform programme, saying public resources must be properly accounted for. "And because this entire reform program is undertaken in the public interest and financed with public resources, every aspect of it must withstand scrutiny," Ruto said. "We welcome scrutiny of every decision and every shilling spent." Ruto said Kenyans should ask questions about government decisions but warned against condemning individuals without evidence. "We must demand answers without prejudice, question decisions without condemning people unheard, and expose wrongdoing wherever it exists," he said. stories.title: Tata Chemicals ordered out of Kenya by president
stories.summary: Image source, Tata Chemicals website Image caption, The factory in Kenya's Magadi is Africa's leading producer of natural soda ash By Nikita Yadav BBC News Published 4 September 2026 One of India's major chemical companies, Tata Chemicals, has been asked to exit Kenya after the government said it had failed to generate enough benefits for the country. President William Ruto has asked the company to "pack up and leave", saying it had been exporting soda ash instead of processing the mineral locally to make glass and chemicals. Ruto said the government had identified new investors to take over the company's operations, with an aim to bring more employment and investment for Kenyans. Tata Chemicals said it respected the government's decision and remains "committed to constructive engagement through the appropriate legal and regulatory channels to resolve the outstanding matters". Ruto made the comments while on a visit to Kajiado county, where Tata Chemicals Magadi's plant is based.

A breakfast here is often incomplete without a cup of chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices. stories.title: Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice in South Africa
stories.summary: Image caption, Abraham Mofokeng was 20 when he joined a peaceful protest in Sharpeville By Pumza Fihlani Reporting from Sharpeville Published 3 September 2026 Abraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators. A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg. "We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government. "All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told." The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted. Mofokeng is now part of a legal case announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.

Photograph: Courtesy of CCF Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves As graduates of an online training course gather from across the continent, the consensus is overwhelming: computers and saving animals go together O n a bitingly cold night in Lapalala Wilderness nature reserve in South Africa’s Limpopo province, Duncan Kanyakera watches as instructor Jacques Viljoen deploys a thermal drone in search of a lone cheetah. Once the drone has disappeared into the inky sky, Kanyakera, from Tsavo in Kenya, and 20 other conservation professionals from across Africa turn their attention to the open-air screen in anticipation. Many of the students – from 11 African countries as far flung as Benin, Liberia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar – witnessing the demonstration have earned their places at Lapalala after performing well on an online training programme for protected area technicians (PAT) run by the Connected Conservation Foundation (CCF).

stories.title: 'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
stories.summary: Image source, Alfred Lasteck / BBC Image caption, Boniface Mgala and a friend were pulled out of a restaurant and attacked by a mob that accused them of stealing a man's genitals By Mungai Ngige ,Â BBC Global Disinformation Unit Â and Â Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Tunduma Published 3 September 2026 More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries. The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media. "They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief. His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen. Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread.

stories.title: New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say
stories.summary: Guinea-Bissau’s transitional president, Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, gestures after voting at a polling station in Bairro de Luanda on Sunday. Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Guinea-Bissau’s transitional president, Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, gestures after voting at a polling station in Bairro de Luanda on Sunday. Photograph: Reuters New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December. According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago. The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

stories.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
stories.summary: A farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa. Photograph: Alamy View image in fullscreen A farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa. Photograph: Alamy Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found. Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network , found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year. Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year.

stories.title: Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’
stories.summary: In her work entitled Holy Gang, artist Puleng Mongale says ‘the sun represents a place where I can meet my ancestors beyond religious limitations’. View image in fullscreen In her work entitled Holy Gang, artist Puleng Mongale says ‘the sun represents a place where I can meet my ancestors beyond religious limitations’. Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’ South African artist Puleng Mongale explores how her childhood church still connects her to the women of her family, not through religion but shared history and memory T his image, called Holy Gang, combines an image of a church in my mother’s home town, Fateng-tse-Ntsho, in Free State province, South Africa , with self-portraits of me, multiplied to form a group of women. Although at first glance the women are moving towards the church, it is not the final destination. Positioned higher, beyond the church, is what appears to be a rising sun.

stories.title: Tunisia's activists decry civil society crackdown
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JrLK Tunisians have been protesting against President Kais Saied this summer, demanding the restoration of democracy and calling for the release of jailed activists and journalists amid a worsening economic and social crisis Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Advertisement "Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities." Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues. "What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention , the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said. Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report , published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely. "It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights . "The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW. He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said.

stories.title: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JxS3 The Ebola outbreak has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it Image: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus , has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it. "Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance," DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo. "Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control," he added. Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities. stories.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pirates manage to board ships operating a long way from the coast and then guide them closer to the shore By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent Published 29 August 2026 Updated 31 August 2026 A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran. Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates. It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade. "Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity." That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north. Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz. And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea.

stories.title: How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand
stories.summary: The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens. Photograph: Courtesy of Water Hub View image in fullscreen The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens. Photograph: Courtesy of Water Hub How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand Scientists say system to treat contaminated wastewater offers a model for ensuring food security in a fast-warming climate A ll it took to turn the murky, heavily polluted waters of South Africa’s Stiebeuel River into a resource clean enough for irrigating a community’s vegetable plots was a collection of stones, heat-treated wood and sand. Without chemicals and using renewable energy, researchers from the University of Cape Town are cleaning 36,000 litres of water, polluted by sewage, chemicals, and traces of drugs and medication, every day to make it usable for growing food in a fast-expanding informal settlement along the course of the river. Scientists behind the project think it could be a model for ensuring food security in the climate crisis. “ What we’re doing is taking that water, treating it every day, and some of that water is now being used for growing vegetables, for feeding hungry children and people living in the informal settlement,” says Kevin Winter, one of the researchers behind the Water Hub project in Langrug , near Stellenbosch in South Africa’s Western Cape region.

stories.summary: The Swedish embassy shut its doors in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, on 31 August. Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy View image in fullscreen The Swedish embassy shut its doors in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, on 31 August. Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Sweden ends aid to Liberia in a hammer blow to women’s rights and healthcare Sexual and reproductive services face an uncertain future as the country’s second-largest donor halts support worth hundreds of millions of pounds T he Swedish flag is still flying above the pale blue building overlooking the Atlantic in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, but the doors of the embassy are now closed to visitors. The billions of kronor of aid that Sweden pipes into the west African country will end on the same day, as sweeping cuts to Swedish development funding come into effect.

stories.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
stories.summary: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation. As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration .

stories.title: ‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach Spain
stories.summary: Composite: Soraya Aybar Laafou View image in fullscreen Composite: Soraya Aybar Laafou ‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach Spain More than two dozen teenagers stuck in the Spanish territory of Ceuta shared their reasons for joining the treacherous mass crossing in July For Fatin, one of the teenage girls now living in limbo in a makeshift camp in the Spanish city of Ceuta, the decision to leave her home in Morocco began to form when she had to give up school. She wanted to continue studying, she says, but at home she was expected to take responsibility for the housework instead. As classes and learning gave way to domestic chores, the future she had imagined for herself began to feel increasingly distant. Fatin was one of 29 girls who shared their feelings about their past and future with the Guardian. All of them had been part of the mass crossing from Morocco in late July that made headlines around the world.
